gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured range or energy-use figure for any recommended pack. The only measured figure on the web for these brands comes from the maker LiTime: an EZ-GO 48V cart carrying one driver went 55.06 miles on 118 Ah of LiTime LiFePO4, about 109.73 Wh per mile. No independent lab or named reviewer has published capacity, range, voltage-sag or amp-draw measurements for Eco Battery, Vatrer, LiTime, Bolt, Allied, RoyPow or Redodo golf-cart packs.
standout_why: I read golfcartshowdown.com (cited), golfcartlab.com brand ranking (cited) and golfcartbatterysource.com buyer's guide (cited), plus golfcartgearlab.com (ranked #2 in results) and cartvolts.com/best-lithium-golf-cart-batteries. None of them reports a measurement. cartvolts says "We don't bench-test batteries; every spec comes from the brand." golfcartgearlab says "we don't test products ourselves." golfcartbatterysource labels its range figures as seller or dealer claims. golfcartshowdown and golfcartlab use only maker specs and their own volts × amp-hours arithmetic. I could not reopen the cited LiTime product page (HTTP 429), so I did not confirm whether it repeats LiTime's blog test.
decides: It does not change the pick by itself. Every rival ranks on maker specs, so a page can honestly say that no pack has an independent edge on measured performance. It can then rank on warranty, BMS amp rating, fitment and price. LiTime's 109.73 Wh/mile maker test gives the reader one way to turn each pack's rated kWh into an expected range on a flat, one-driver run. That is about 49 miles for a 5,376 Wh pack (Eco 105Ah, Vatrer 105Ah) and about 47 miles for a 5,120 Wh pack (LiTime 100Ah, Redodo 100Ah). This narrows the 105Ah-versus-100Ah gap to about 2 miles. That makes a case for the cheaper 100Ah packs (LiTime $999.99 as ChatGPT showed it, or Dealectric's Redodo kit) over $2,300–2,700 premium kits, where the shopper's cart does not need more than 200 A.

findings.label: Maker's real-world range test: distance on one charge
findings.value: 55.06 miles from near full charge (118 Ah)
findings.source_title: [Full Guide] How Many Ah Batteries Do I Need for a Golf Cart (LiTime, David Lee, Jul 8 2026)
findings.note: LiTime ran this test on its own product, so it is not independent. Method as stated: one driver, no passengers; drive for 1 hour, rest 20 minutes, then measure voltage, repeating until the end. The post does not give speed, terrain or temperature. The pack is two 60Ah units in parallel, not the 100Ah model ChatGPT showed.

findings.label: Maker-measured energy use per mile
findings.source_title: [Full Guide] How Many Ah Batteries Do I Need for a Golf Cart (LiTime)
findings.note: LiTime's formula is 51.2 V × 118 Ah ÷ 55.06 mi = 109.73 Wh/mi (6,041.6 Wh ÷ 55.06). My extrapolation, not a measurement: 5,376 Wh (51.2 V × 105 Ah) ÷ 109.73 ≈ 49.0 mi; 5,120 Wh (51.2 V × 100 Ah) ÷ 109.73 ≈ 46.7 mi. This assumes the same cart, one driver, unknown terrain and full usable capacity.
